question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, in metres per second, to the exact defined value?

subquestions: What is the exact defined value of the speed of light in vacuum (c) in metres per second?

observations.content:
Summary: The speed of light in vacuum, c, is exactly 299,792,458 m/s, and this value defines the metre in the International System of Units (SI). This fixed value ensures the metre is defined as the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

### Relativity [...] ### Relativity

The speed of light in vacuum is constant, regardless of the motion of the source or the inertial reference frame of the observer.

### Speed

The speed of light in vacuum, c, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of speed, the metre per second.

The fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum, c, is defined exactly:

c \mspace{4mu} = 299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458 \ \text{m} \ \text{s}^{-1} [...] Inverting this relation gives an exact expression for the metre per second in terms of the speed of light in vacuum, c :

1 \mspace{4mu} \text{m} \mspace{4mu} \text{s}^{-1} \mspace{4mu} = \dfrac{1}{299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458} \mspace{4mu} c\\  

### Length or distance

The speed of light in vacuum, c, together with the hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom, ΔνCs, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of length, the metre.

# Standard Definition of speed of light and metre

The speed of light is the speed at which lightwaves propagate through different materials. In particular, the value for the speed of light in a vacuum is now defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. [...] On the other hand, if you say: the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299.792.458 meters per second, then, in order to avoid circularity, you need a definition of a meter independent from the speed of light. This was the status before 1983. Since then, the definition of a meter places 0 error on speed of light in vacuum.

DanielC's user avatar [...] Since the speed of light in a vacuum is a constant, both are true. As long as we know what a second is. As for which came first, the speed of light in a vacuum was established to be 299,792,458 metres per second in 1975, and in 1983 the International System of Units (SI) redefined the metre as the distance light in a vacuum travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This redefining did away with the margin of error in the speed of light.
